title: ILTACON 2026: Context is King — But Transformation is Still the Hard Part
author: Legal IT Insider

kp.k: Legal AI is shifting toward context-rich, matter-centric systems
kp.d: The September 2, 2026 conference report identifies context engineering as a dominant theme across vendor announcements and interviews. NetDocuments launched its Legal Context Graph in May; iManage's forthcoming platform, scheduled for general availability in October, uses a Context Fabric to enrich and connect document information; Harvey is organising work around matters, memory and preferences. These are reported product directions rather than measured improvements in legal work. Mallesons' Michelle Mahoney describes using Harvey's memory capabilities to incorporate firm and individual context, including voice and tone.
qs: Virtually every major AI announcement in the run up to and during the conference centred on providing legal AI systems with the information, history and organisational knowledge needed to become a useful assistant.
Harvey II is centred around the matter, context, best practices and preferences.
Rather than lawyers repeatedly starting from scratch, Harvey is increasingly organising work around matters, memory, preferences and institutional knowledge.

kp.k: Clean data is a prerequisite for useful AI
kp.d: The author argues that context-dependent AI makes data hygiene urgent. Drawing on Wilson Sonsini's CRM work with Salesforce, CIO Jeffrey Lolley identifies securing clean data and persuading people of its value as the main challenge, rather than technology implementation. iManage CEO Neil Araujo likewise reports that customers are focused on preparing data for AI. These are practitioner and vendor observations, not quantified implementation findings.
qs: If ever there was an imperative for firms to do the hard yards when it comes to data hygiene it is now.
Getting people to understand the value and getting clean data has been the biggest challenge.
You hear about people who went out, bought the first thing available and sat it on top of data that wasn’t clean. The data needs to be the first part.

kp.k: Autonomous agents may substantially increase governance risks
kp.d: The report frames governance as an enabler of adoption rather than an obstacle. Intapp co-founder and chief product officer Thad Jampol predicts that moving from question-and-answer tools to autonomous agents will increase compliance risks 'by an order of magnitude'; this is his forecast, not a measured risk estimate. The Intapp–Legora partnership connects Legora with Intapp Walls and Intapp Time for protected workflows and automated AI time capture, addressing information held beyond document management systems.
qs: Governance is notably no longer being viewed or positioned as a brake on innovation, but the enabler of broader adoption.
Governance challenges will get worse before they get better. As we move away from ‘question and answer’ and have autonomous agents doing work that increases compliance risks by an order of magnitude.
everything done in Legora is protected by ethical walls.

kp.k: Access controls increasingly encode client and matter restrictions
kp.d: iManage announced the ability to disable AI at client or matter level to meet outside counsel guidelines and client requirements. Wilson Sonsini described building an architecture that would automatically determine appropriate data access, rather than requiring lawyers to decide whether information could be used in each context. These examples concern technical enforcement of access permissions, not removal of human verification of legal outputs.
qs: Other notable announcements included iManage’s new platform’s ability to disable AI at the client or matter level to accommodate outside counsel guidelines and client requirements.
We wanted to build an engine that could make that decision for our lawyers and give them access appropriately, taking that decision-making out of the hands of lawyers.

kp.k: Agents target administrative and multi-step legal workflows
kp.d: The report describes agentic experimentation across the business and practice of law. Aderant announced early access to its Agent Center, with seven agents across appeals, collection, talent and time, and Lisa Erickson reported another eight to ten in development. Intapp's Celeste handles intake, including emails, and is available in the UK and US; Jampol claims its customer pipeline is the largest in company history. Litera describes matter-lifecycle coverage, Harvey longer-running matter-centric workflows, Opus 2 case management and dispute resolution agents, and LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters multi-tool workflow harnesses. These are announcements and executive claims, not demonstrated productivity results.
qs: Aderant has seven agents across appeals, collection, talent and time
Rather than general purpose AI tools, agents start with the firms own business context.
Harvey discussed its agentic capabilities built around longer-running workflows and matter-centric work management – each matter has a vault, agent centre, library and task list.
Opus 2 launched its agentic AI framework Ingenuity to provide AI agents for legal case management and dispute resolution.

kp.k: Interoperability supports firms' choice of AI ecosystems
kp.d: The report presents MCP integrations as a way to connect legal data, tools and workflows across products. iManage's Thomson Reuters integration surfaces content in CoCounsel and is expected to improve HighQ integration; Litera connects customer data and workflows to Lito; NetDocuments takes an AI-tool-agnostic approach. Against an increasingly complex market, including Google's announced Gemini for Legal launch, the author argues that firms need to construct their own ecosystems.
qs: Litera enables customers to connect their data and workflows with Lito using MCP.
NetDocuments has an open, AI-tool-agnostic approach to MCP that allows customers to connect to the tools they choose.
With Google announcing during ILTACON the launch of Gemini for Legal, the landscape is ever more complex, and law firms need to be able to create their own ecosystem.

kp.k: Human verification erodes AI's expected efficiency gains
kp.d: The author reports that substantial adoption has not necessarily produced net time savings or cost recovery because checking AI output duplicates effort. Actionstep chief product officer Triona Buckley attributes incomplete efficiency gains to continuing human review requirements and highlights audit trails, agent-activity tracking and permissions. The article supplies no quantified review burden, time-saving estimate or study sample.
qs: Despite substantial AI adoption, many organisations are still wrestling with a ‘verification tax’ that takes away from time savings, meaning that firms are doubling up on effort and time and not recouping costs.

Actionstep’s chief product officer [Triona Buckley](https://nz.linkedin.com/in/trionabuckleysaunders) noted that firms have not yet fully realised efficiency gains because significant human review remains necessary.
You need an audit trail and the ability to track what agents are doing.

kp.k: Consumption pricing could alter AI deployment economics
kp.d: The report identifies token costs as a newly prominent issue and suggests subsidised experimentation is ending. Control Risks partner Brad Kolacinski anticipates frontier models moving toward token charging. Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg predicts continued price increases from infrastructure constraints and asserts that additional computing power cannot be bought before 2029. These are attributed expectations, not established cost trajectories. Harvey is preparing through performance benchmarking, while NetDocuments' Michael Hill frames the issue as optimising effectiveness and value per dollar.
qs: A topic that barely featured last year emerged repeatedly this year: tokenomics, for want of a better word.
The days of subsidised AI experimentation looks to be ending.

Weinberg suggested that frontier model prices will keep going up thanks to constraints on infrastructure – you can’t buy more computing power before 2029 because demand for AI exceeds our ability to build and power new data centres.
Harvey is focusing heavily on benchmarking performance and “building the muscle to prepare for these changes.”

kp.k: Pricing and integration discussions increasingly focus on value
kp.d: Hike2's Catherine Krow claims that movement away from hourly billing is now occurring, with new opportunities for law firms and legal departments to discuss value. The report supplies no adoption rate or specific replacement pricing model. Opensity's Andrew Dober describes a shift from selecting practice technologies toward integrating platforms and data to generate organisational ROI. Neither observation establishes a measured market-wide pricing or productivity change.
qs: For the first time we are seeing a move off the billable hour.
People have solved what technology they want to use, but how does it work together and drive ROI that helps them evolve as an organisation?
Historically people focused on use of technology in practice. Now there is more engagement around one platform and how data comes together.

kp.k: Transformation requires workflow redesign, not simply software deployment
kp.d: The author's central conclusion is that technological progress alone is insufficient: firms must change how work is performed. Epiq managing director Kieron Champion questions whether deployed and licensed tools are delivering user value and argues that only the most mature firms are pursuing genuine transformation. His diagnosis centres on weak adoption, unchanged processes and failure to distinguish tasks AI can perform from work requiring humans in the loop or in the lead. This is an interview-based assessment rather than a systematic maturity evaluation.
qs: I think only the most mature firms around this AI journey are looking to transform the way work is done.
Major progress was evident everywhere this year at ILTACON, but firms have to change the way they work to fully take advantage of it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article portrays legal AI as moving toward contextual, matter-centric and agentic work, while arguing that verification, governance, costs and organisational change constrain the benefits.
pts.d:
Context and data: NetDocuments CEO Josh Baxter predicts agents will accelerate work but require context. The article describes iManage's forthcoming platform as enriching and linking document information to improve retrieval and interrogation. Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg characterises 2026 as a year of transformation, with the second half focused on matter-centric and personalised AI; chief product officer Anique Drumright describes Harvey II in those terms. Mallesons chief innovation officer Michelle Mahoney reports work on firm and individual memory to support the firm's voice and tone. Wilson Sonsini CIO Jeffrey Lolley identifies clean data and persuading people of its value as harder than the technology itself.

Governance: Intapp chief product officer Thad Jampol predicts substantially greater compliance risks as autonomous agents replace question-and-answer interactions. The article reports protections through Intapp ethical walls and iManage's planned client- or matter-level AI disabling. Lolley describes Wilson Sonsini building an architecture that determines appropriate data access rather than leaving those decisions to lawyers.

Agentic work and integration: Aderant's Lisa Erickson announces seven back-office agents and another eight to ten in development. The article describes Intapp Celeste as handling intake, including emails, and reducing administrative burdens. It attributes to Litera CEO Avaneesh Marwaha the claim that Lito spans the matter lifecycle from intake to close. It reports Harvey's longer-running, matter-centric workflows, Opus 2's case-management and dispute-resolution agents, and LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters approaches to combining tools in workflows. MCP integrations are presented as enabling firms to connect content, tools and workflows into their own ecosystems.

Efficiency and cost: The article argues that human verification can absorb AI time savings, duplicate effort and prevent cost recovery. It attributes to Actionstep chief product officer Triona Buckley the observation that significant human review has prevented firms from fully realising efficiency gains. Control Risks partner Brad Kolacinski predicts a shift toward token-based pricing that will change the economics of AI use. Weinberg predicts increasing frontier-model prices because of infrastructure constraints and claims additional computing power cannot be bought before 2029. NetDocuments' Michael Hill argues for more effective AI that reaches answers faster and delivers greater value per dollar.

Pricing and transformation: Hike2 principal Catherine Krow reports seeing a move away from billable hours and opportunities for different value conversations between law firms and departments. Opensity's Andrew Dober describes a shift from selecting technology toward integration and organisational ROI. Epiq managing director Kieron Champion argues that licensing tools without redesigning processes or deciding where AI and humans belong will not deliver full value; he thinks only the most mature firms are pursuing work transformation. The article concludes that firms must change how they work to take full advantage of AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of conference interviews, executive observations, product announcements and named implementation examples, rather than quantified studies.
pts.d: Legal IT Insider synthesises conversations with vendor executives, advisers and law-firm leaders. Product announcements provide examples of the direction of development, but the article does not report independent tests of their capabilities or measured client outcomes. Mallesons' work with Harvey and Wilson Sonsini's CRM and access-governance architecture supply concrete organisational examples. Buckley's account of review burdens, Krow's observation about billing, Dober's integration observations and Champion's concerns about licence deployment are professional or customer-facing assessments; no sample sizes, time-savings calculations, pricing shares or ROI measurements are supplied. Jampol's 'order of magnitude' compliance-risk claim and Weinberg's infrastructure and price predictions are attributed executive judgments without supporting calculations or infrastructure data in the article. Harvey's focus on benchmarking is mentioned, but no benchmark, methodology or score is reported. Jampol's assertion that Celeste has Intapp's largest-ever customer pipeline is a demand indicator claimed by its supplier, not evidence of realised productivity.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Claims centre on the September 2026 conference period, with specific near-term product milestones and a longer infrastructure constraint prediction extending to 2029.
pts.d: The article, dated 2 September 2026, describes a three-year progression from generative-AI curiosity through pilots and firm-wide rollouts to agentic experimentation. It reports NetDocuments' Legal Context Graph launch in May and iManage's forthcoming general availability in October. Weinberg places matter-centric personalisation in the second half of 2026. Erickson's seven-agent commitment is for the end of the conference; the additional eight to ten agents have no stated delivery date. Celeste is described as already available in the UK and US, while Aderant Agent Center is in early access. Jampol conditions worsening compliance risks on increasingly capable and widely adopted autonomous agents. Verification burdens are presented as ongoing, with no end date. Token-based pricing changes are anticipated rather than assigned a definite transition date; Weinberg links continuing price increases to infrastructure shortages and invokes 2029 for additional computing availability. Full benefits are conditional on clean data, contextual information, appropriate access controls, integration, process redesign and explicit decisions about human review and leadership.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms, practising lawyers, back-office teams, technology and governance leaders, and corporate legal buyers.
pts.d: Lawyers are promised more contextual assistance, persistent matter knowledge and multi-step workflows, but still face verification work. Intake and other administrative teams are targets for automation; Aderant identifies appeals, collection, talent and time among its agent areas. Firm technology, knowledge-management and governance leaders must clean and connect data, manage permissions, track agent actions and integrate multiple suppliers. Firm management faces licence-value questions, consumption costs, ROI measurement and process redesign. Clients influence AI deployment through outside counsel guidelines and matter-specific requirements; law departments are included in Krow's claim about new value and pricing conversations. The article distinguishes more mature firms pursuing transformation from firms merely distributing licences. Named firm examples include Mallesons and Wilson Sonsini, but the article does not quantify effects by firm size, predict staffing reductions, or make access-to-justice claims.
